title: Euclidean Fourier symbol product and first-order remainder
statement:
Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] and the symbol estimates and oscillatory-integral normalization of [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators]. Let $m\geq1$, $p,q,t\geq0$ and $r,s\in\mathbf Z$. Let $a\in S^r(\mathbf R^m;\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q))$ and $c\in S^s(\mathbf R^m;\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^q,\mathbf C^t))$ both have compact $x$ support. Put $\widehat a_x(\eta,\xi)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}a(y,\xi)\,dy$. The absolutely convergent integral $$q(x,\xi)=(2\pi)^{-m}\int e^{ix\cdot\eta}c(x,\xi+\eta)\widehat a_x(\eta,\xi)\,d\eta$$ defines a smooth symbol $q\in S^{r+s}$ compactly supported in $x$, satisfying $q-ca\in S^{r+s-1}$. For every real $\lambda,\mu,
u,	au\in C_c^\infty(\mathbf R^m)$ there is a symbol $q_{\lambda\mu
u}\in S^{r+s}$ compactly supported in $x$ such that $$\lambda\operatorname{Op}(c)\mu
u\operatorname{Op}(a)	au=\operatorname{Op}(q_{\lambda\mu
u})	au,\qquad q_{\lambda\mu
u}-\lambda\mu
u ca\in S^{r+s-1}.$$ These are identities on all distributions for the localized transposes with both spatial cutoffs. For real operators replace each input symbol by $a_{\mathbf R}(x,\xi)=(a(x,\xi)+\overline{a(x,-\xi)})/2$ and similarly for $c$; the same formula and estimates hold for their real distributional actions.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5) and Proposition 3.7, printed pp.12–13. Composition Proposition 3.7: Euclidean Fourier product and its first Taylor remainder. Agent-supplied local formulation. Supplemental course read online: https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3, (3.3)–(3.6), 3.12–3.15, printed pp.6–12; coordinate-change and amplitude reduction details are supplied by the agent, not asserted to be proved in those notes.

proof.text:
Write $w(v)=1+|v|$, $A(\eta,\xi)=\widehat a_x(\eta,\xi)$, and call the requested symbol $Q$ to distinguish it from the rank $q$. Compact spatial support means one compact set for all frequencies. Local symbol estimates become global by taking a compact neighbourhood of this support; derivatives vanish off it. For each multi-index $\beta$, apply [lem-sfb-compact-symbol-frequency-kernel] to the compactly supported symbol $\partial_\xi^\beta a$ of order $r-|\beta|$. Its Fourier variable is $\eta/(2\pi)$, so it gives
$$\|\partial_\xi^\beta A(\eta,\xi)\|\leq C_{\beta L}w(\eta)^{-L}w(\xi)^{r-|\beta|}\quad(L\geq0).$$
Differentiation commutes with the spatial integral: on compact parameter neighbourhoods every integrand derivative is bounded by a constant times the indicator of the common compact support. That indicator is integrable by [lem-sfb-continuous-on-compact-integrable]. Iterated [lem-sfb-dominated-integral-frechet-derivative] gives the derivative formulas, including $\eta$ derivatives inserting powers of $-iy$; [lem-sfb-oscillatory-cutoff-convergence] gives continuity of these derivatives. Thus $A$ is smooth. All uses are entrywise, and finite matrices give the norm estimates.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.10, (3.11), printed p.9. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
For $0\leq\theta\leq1$ the triangle inequality gives
$$w(\xi+\theta\eta)\leq w(\xi)w(\eta),\qquad
w(\xi)\leq w(\xi+\theta\eta)w(\eta).$$
Raise the first inequality to $u$ if $u\geq0$, or take the reciprocal of the second to the power $-u$ if $u<0$. Consequently
$$w(\xi+\theta\eta)^u\leq w(\xi)^u w(\eta)^{|u|}\quad(u\in\mathbf Z).$$
This handles negative as well as positive symbol orders.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, Peetre estimate following (3.15), printed p.11. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
By Leibniz, each formal derivative term of $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta Q$ has integrand
$$e^{ix\cdot\eta}(i\eta)^{\alpha-\gamma}
(\partial_x^\gamma\partial_\xi^\delta c)(x,\xi+\eta)
(\partial_\xi^{\beta-\delta}A)(\eta,\xi),
\quad\gamma\leq\alpha,\ \delta\leq\beta.$$
Steps 1–2 bound this by
$$Cw(\xi)^{r+s-|\beta|}
w(\eta)^{-L+|\alpha-\gamma|+|s-|\delta||}.$$
Choose $L>m+|\alpha|+\max_{\delta\leq\beta}|s-|\delta||$, increasing it for any further derivative. For $d>m$, $w(\eta)^{-d}\leq(1+|\eta|^2)^{-d/2}$ is integrable by [lem-sfb-euclidean-bracket-integrable]. The entrywise majorant estimate proves absolute convergence and the integrated order bound. Locally in $(x,\xi)$, the factor involving $\xi$ is bounded; iterated dominated differentiation therefore justifies every formal derivative, and dominated convergence gives its continuity. Hence $Q$ is smooth and belongs to $S^{r+s}$. Outside the common compact spatial support of $c$ the integrand is zero, so $Q$ has compact spatial support.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, derivatives of (3.15), printed p.11. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
For fixed $\xi$, $a(\cdot,\xi)$ is entrywise compactly supported smooth, hence Schwartz. Schwartz Fourier inversion, with $\eta=2\pi\theta$ and Jacobian $(2\pi)^m$, gives
$$a(x,\xi)=(2\pi)^{-m}\int e^{ix\cdot\eta}A(\eta,\xi)\,d\eta.$$
Subtract $c(x,\xi)$ times this absolutely convergent integral from $Q$. The fundamental theorem of calculus on $\theta\mapsto c(x,\xi+\theta\eta)$ yields the exact formula
$$Q-ca=(2\pi)^{-m}\int e^{ix\cdot\eta}
\left[\sum_{j=1}^m\eta_j\int_0^1
(\partial_{\xi_j}c)(x,\xi+\theta\eta)\,d\theta\right]
A(\eta,\xi)\,d\eta.$$
The interval integrands are continuous. Products remain in the displayed matrix order, with $c$ multiplying $a$ on the left.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, Taylor formula and Fourier inversion, pp.11–12, expansion index p=0. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
In a derivative term of $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta(Q-ca)$, let $\gamma,\delta$ be the derivatives falling on $c$. The bracket in step 4 is bounded by
$$Cw(\eta)w(\xi)^{s-1-|\delta|}w(\eta)^{|s-1-|\delta||}.$$
This follows by applying step 2 to $\partial_x^\gamma\partial_\xi^{\delta+e_j}c$, uniformly for $\theta\in[0,1]$, whose interval has length one. Including phase derivatives and step 1 bounds the full integrand by
$$Cw(\xi)^{r+s-1-|\beta|}
w(\eta)^{-L+1+|\alpha-\gamma|+|s-1-|\delta||}.$$
Choose $L$ so the last exponent is less than $-m$ for all finitely many derivative terms, and for further derivatives as needed. Bracket integrability and the entrywise integral estimate give
$$\|\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta(Q-ca)\|
\leq C_{\alpha\beta}w(\xi)^{r+s-1-|\beta|}.$$
Dominated differentiation over $[0,1]$ uses a constant majorant on each compact parameter neighbourhood; over $\eta$ it uses the displayed integrable bound. Dominated convergence gives continuity. Thus this proves the estimates for every derivative of the remainder, exactly $Q-ca\in S^{r+s-1}$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, Taylor remainder, pp.11–12, expansion index p=0. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
For a compactly supported smooth input $f$, put $H_f(\xi)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\xi}f(y)\,dy$. Schwartz inclusion and Fourier invariance make $H_f$ rapidly decreasing. The compact-symbol theorem gives $g=\operatorname{Op}(a)f$ compactly supported smooth and, changing from its $2\pi$ convention,
$$H_g(\zeta)=(2\pi)^{-m}\int A(\zeta-\xi,\xi)H_f(\xi)\,d\xi.$$
Apply that theorem's quantization formula to $c$ and $g$. The double integral for $\operatorname{Op}(c)g$ has coefficient $(2\pi)^{-2m}$. Translate $\eta=\zeta-\xi$, with Jacobian one. Its norm is bounded by
$$Cw(\eta)^{-L+|s|}w(\xi)^{r+s}|H_f(\xi)|.$$
The first factor is integrable for $L>m+|s|$; rapid decay bounds the second by $Cw(\xi)^{-d}$ for $d>m$. The product-integrability and Fubini node therefore allows swapping the integrals. The inner $\eta$ integral equals $(2\pi)^mQ(x,\xi)$, leaving
$$(2\pi)^{-m}\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}Q(x,\xi)H_f(\xi)\,d\xi
=\operatorname{Op}(Q)f(x).$$
The final equality is the compact-symbol theorem applied to the symbol from step 3. This proves equality of the specified oscillatory quantizations, including their cutoff limits.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, derivation of (3.15), pp.10–11. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
Set $h=\mu\nu$, $b=ha$ and $d=\lambda c$. Leibniz shows that $b\in S^r$, $d\in S^s$ with compact spatial support: every derivative of a fixed smooth compactly supported cutoff is bounded. Output multiplication multiplies the quantization symbol directly in its defining integral. Apply steps 1–6 to $(b,d)$ and call the result $q_{\lambda\mu\nu}=Q_{d,b}$. It is independent of $\tau$. For a test $f$, $\tau f$ is a test and
$$\lambda\operatorname{Op}(c)\mu\nu\operatorname{Op}(a)(\tau f)
=\operatorname{Op}(d)\operatorname{Op}(b)(\tau f)
=\operatorname{Op}(q_{\lambda\mu\nu})(\tau f).$$
The symbol has compact spatial support, order $r+s$, and
$$q_{\lambda\mu\nu}-db
=q_{\lambda\mu\nu}-\lambda\mu\nu ca\in S^{r+s-1}$$
by step 5.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3.14, localized composition, p.10. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
Use only the test-function and transpose continuity clause of [lem-sfb-compact-oscillatory-amplitude-reduction], not its reduced-symbol conclusion. Apply it to
$$\lambda(x)c(x,\xi)\mu(y),\quad
\nu(x)a(x,\xi)\tau(y),\quad
q_{\lambda\mu\nu}(x,\xi)\tau(y).$$
All three amplitudes have compact $(x,y)$ support and satisfy the required estimates by Leibniz and the established symbol bounds. It follows that
$$L_c=\lambda\operatorname{Op}(c)\mu,\quad
L_a=\nu\operatorname{Op}(a)\tau,\quad
L_Q=\operatorname{Op}(q_{\lambda\mu\nu})\tau$$
and their bilinear transposes act continuously on test functions, with compact support controlled by the relevant spatial projection. Their transpose extensions are precisely the localized distributional actions in the definition. In particular $L_a^tL_c^t\phi$ is a legitimate compactly supported smooth test for every test $\phi$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, localized interpretation of §3.3–3.9; continuity supplied by the cited amplitude node. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
Step 7 gives $L_cL_af=L_Qf$ for all tests $f$. Pair with a test $\phi$ and use the defining transpose identities:
$$\int f\cdot(L_a^tL_c^t\phi-L_Q^t\phi)=0\quad\text{for every test }f.$$
The parenthesized difference is smooth with compact support by step 8. Testing a component against its complex conjugate gives a zero integral of its squared absolute value. Continuity then forces that component to vanish everywhere. Thus $L_a^tL_c^t\phi=L_Q^t\phi$. For every distribution $u$ the definition yields
$$(L_cL_au)(\phi)=u(L_a^tL_c^t\phi)
=u(L_Q^t\phi)=(L_Qu)(\phi).$$
This proves the asserted equality on all distributions by transposition with both spatial cutoffs.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, Proposition 3.7; supplemental course read online at https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, localized transpose extension of §3.14; explicit duality argument by Q83. Expanded argument by Q83.

proof.text:
Put $a^
atural(x,\xi)=\overline{a(x,-\xi)}$, $a_{\mathbf R}=(a+a^
atural)/2$, and similarly for $c$. Reflection and conjugation preserve all symbol bounds and compact spatial supports. On real inputs, conjugating the quantization integral and substituting $\xi\mapsto-\xi$ gives $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Op}(a)=\operatorname{Op}(a_{\mathbf R})$, also the real-action clause of the amplitude node. Apply the construction to the two symmetrized input symbols. Indeed
$$A_{a^
atural}(\eta,\xi)=\overline{A_a(-\eta,-\xi)},\qquad
Q_{c^
atural,a^
atural}(x,\xi)=\overline{Q_{c,a}(x,-\xi)}.$$
The second identity follows by conjugating the absolutely convergent integral and substituting $\eta\mapsto-\eta$, whose absolute Jacobian is one. Thus natural-fixed inputs give a natural-fixed output, and real cutoffs preserve this property. Steps 3 and 5 give the same estimates with leading product $c_{\mathbf R}a_{\mathbf R}$. The transpose equalities restrict to real tests and real distributions. All formulas also hold in zero ranks: the matrices and all integrals are then zero.
